name: spica
label: Spica (alpha Virginis)
sources: [HE71] Herbison-Evans, Hanbury Brown, Davis & Allen 1971, MNRAS 151, 161: Narrabri intensity-interferometer orbit (theta_A = 0.90 +/- 0.04 mas, a, i, Omega = 131.6 +/- 2.1)
[T16] Tkachenko et al. 2016, MNRAS 458, 1964: masses, radii, Teffs, i = 63.1
Bailey et al. 2019 (polarimetric orbit): Omega 130.4 +/- 6.8 confirms the retrograde sense
Harrington et al. 2016, A&A 590, A54: e 0.108 +/- 0.014, omega (secondary) 232 +/- 1 deg, K1 121.1, K2 189.8 km/s
Robinette & Aufdenberg: apsidal period 139 +/- 6 yr (HE71: 124 +/- 11 yr)
notes: The primary is a beta Cep pulsator and tidally distorted (ellipsoidal, non-eclipsing at i = 63): rendered as a static sphere.
The i-band anchor is the anchored-blackbody colour of a ~25 kK photosphere (+/- ~0.1 mag; only shifts the red zero point).
semimajor_au from Kepler's third law with the [T16] masses.

Eccentric orbit: e 0.108 +/- 0.014 (Harrington et al. 2016; 0.125 in their other solution), arg_periastron_deg 232 +/- 1 for the SECONDARY (Harrington 2016), which is hbtsim's convention (the secondary's relative orbit). If the 232 is the primary's spectroscopic omega the value here should be 52 (flagged).

Apsidal motion: the periastron advances with a period of 139 +/- 6 yr (Robinette & Aufdenberg) or 124 +/- 11 yr (Herbison-Evans et al. 1971); since the 1971 Narrabri orbit it has moved by ~142 deg, so omega(1971) ~ 90 deg in this convention. Periastron epoch JD 2454189.4 (Tkachenko 2016); BinarySystem carries no epoch, so a campaign's options.phase0 sets the phase of the first night.
Spica Ac (GRAVITY 2026, 111 mas, 1.4 Msun) contributes negligible light.

summary.sources: Herbison-Evans et al. 1971; Tkachenko et al. 2016
